score_rationale: Strong willingness-to-pay validated by active commercial B2B database market with at least 8 major vendors currently selling event planner and wedding coordinator databases: Exact Data (comprehensive wedding planner email list database with contact information for professional wedding planners, event planners, and bridal consultants nationwide), LISTGIANT (event organizers mailing list with verified contact details for professionals who decide which vendors are booked), InfoGlobalData (event planner email list with well-segmented access to event planners, event coordinators, wedding planners, corporate event planners), DataCaptive (event planners email list with up-to-date verified contacts of professional event planners, coordinators, and industry decision-makers), Accurate Info (event planner mailing list to reach target audience effectively), Averick Media (event planner email list with database of event planners in USA), BizInfor USA (event organizer mailing list with 20,000+ verified records), and Blue Mail Media (event organizers email list with 95% deliverability rate and over a decade of experience). Commercial vendors report lists updated every 90 days with full CCPA, GDPR, CAN-SPAM compliance and segmentation by event type (corporate events, weddings, conferences, festivals, non-profit events) across US, UK, Canada, Australia, EMEA, and APAC markets, indicating sustained international B2B demand. Four high-value B2B buyer segments with strong LTV justification: (1) Event management software and planning platforms (Cvent event management software for corporate events and conferences at $1,500-$10,000+/year depending on event volume and attendee count, Eventbrite ticketing and event marketing platform charging 3.7% + $1.79 per paid ticket with high-volume planners generating $5,000-$50,000/year in platform fees, Planning Pod all-in-one event planning software at $39-$99/month = $468-$1,188/year, Social Tables event diagramming and seating at $125-$500/month = $1,500-$6,000/year, Bizzabo event experience platform for enterprise conferences, Whova event app and management, Tripleseat venue and catering management for banquet sales, Honeybook client management for wedding planners at $19-$39/month = $228-$468/year) selling SaaS subscriptions at $500-$50,000/year per event planner depending on event scale and frequency (wedding planners doing 20 weddings/year = $2,000/year software spend, corporate event planners managing 50+ conferences/year = $20,000/year) with typical 3-7 year customer lifetime generating $6,000-$350,000 LTV where one acquired mid-tier planner ($5,000/year contract) justifies $1,000-$2,000 CAC making $79-$99 database deliver 10×-25× cost savings; (2) Event venues and hospitality providers (hotels, conference centers, wedding venues, banquet halls, country clubs, wineries, historic estates, outdoor event spaces) paying commission or lead fees to event planners who book their venues at 10-20% commission on venue rental fees ($5,000-$50,000 wedding venue = $500-$10,000 planner commission, $20,000-$100,000 corporate conference = $2,000-$20,000 commission) making venues willing to invest $500-$2,000 in planner outreach and relationship development to secure bookings where one wedding or conference justifies 5×-200× marketing spend vs. $79-$99 database; (3) Event vendor services and suppliers (catering companies providing food service at $50-$200/person for 100-500 guest events = $5,000-$100,000 catering contracts, audio-visual and production companies renting sound systems, lighting, projectors, LED walls at $2,000-$50,000 per event, floral designers and decorators at $1,000-$20,000 per wedding or gala, event rental companies providing tables, chairs, linens, tents at $2,000-$30,000, photographers and videographers at $2,000-$10,000, entertainment and DJ services at $1,000-$10,000, transportation and shuttle services, photo booth rentals, event staffing agencies) selling services to event planners who control vendor selection and procurement for client events where one event planner booking 30 weddings/year at $3,000 average floral spend = $90,000/year recurring customer value for florist justifying $5,000-$10,000 relationship investment making $79-$99 database deliver 50×-126× cost savings; and (4) Event technology and experiential vendors (live streaming and virtual event platforms for hybrid conferences, event registration and ticketing software, mobile event apps, audience engagement tools, event analytics and ROI tracking, RFID and NFC badge systems for conferences, interactive displays and touchscreens, virtual reality and AR experiences, live polling and Q&A platforms, event networking software) selling per-event technology packages at $1,000-$20,000 or annual platform subscriptions at $5,000-$50,000 where corporate event planners managing 20-100 events/year generate $50,000-$500,000 in annual technology spend creating strong buyer LTV. Secondary buyer segments include: event insurance providers (cancellation insurance, liability coverage, weather insurance for outdoor events), event marketing and promotion agencies, printing services (invitations, programs, signage, name badges), gift and swag suppliers (branded merchandise, welcome bags, conference swag), travel management companies (group hotel blocks, attendee travel coordination), and professional services (event accountants, contract attorneys, event liability consultants). Large total addressable market: approximately 80,000-120,000 professional event planning companies and independent event coordinators operating in United States (per US Bureau of Labor Statistics and industry association estimates), with segmentation across wedding planners (30,000-40,000 specializing in weddings and social events), corporate event planners (20,000-30,000 managing conferences, trade shows, corporate meetings, product launches), non-profit event coordinators (10,000-15,000 managing charity galas, fundraisers, auctions), party planners (10,000-15,000 focusing on birthday parties, anniversaries, milestone celebrations), and specialized planners (10,000-20,000 managing festivals, concerts, sporting events, experiential marketing activations). This creates 100,000-150,000 total prospect companies/independents with 150,000-250,000 decision-maker contacts (business owners, lead planners, event coordinators, venue sales managers). Partial public data availability: most states do not require occupational licensing for event planners or wedding coordinators (no centralized regulatory database), but public business entity registrations exist (Secretary of State LLC and corporation filings for event planning companies with "event planning", "wedding", "party planning", "conference management" in business names), business license registries (city/county business licenses for event planning services), and industry certifications (Certified Meeting Professional CMP credential holders published by Events Industry Council, Certified Special Events Professional CSEP by ISES, Wedding Planning Institute certified wedding planner directories). Better data sources include: business directories (Google Business listings for "event planners" by city, Yelp event planning category, The Knot and WeddingWire vendor directories for wedding planners with public business profiles and contact info), venue preferred vendor lists (many venues publish recommended planner lists), and industry association member directories (Meeting Professionals International MPI, International Live Events Association ILEA, American Society of Association Executives ASAE, National Association of Catering and Events NACE members). Engineering lift is moderate: scrape Secretary of State business registries filtering for event planning business name patterns, parse city business license databases, aggregate industry certification holder directories (CMP, CSEP), scrape business directory listings (Google, Yelp, The Knot vendor search, WeddingWire directory with 100,000+ wedding vendors), cross-reference venue preferred vendor lists, harvest industry association member directories, enrich with website scraping and social media (Instagram wedding planner accounts, LinkedIn event planner profiles), geocode addresses, classify by specialization (wedding/corporate/non-profit/party/festival), normalize company size estimates based on employee count and annual event volume, deduplicate multi-city operators. No affordable flat-file competitor exists below $79 on Gumroad — all existing vendors (8+ identified) use per-contact pricing or require enterprise sales contact for quotes, with typical event industry B2B list pricing at $0.20-$0.60 per contact ($16,000-$90,000 for 150,000 records) making $79-$99 one-time CSV deliver 161×-1,139× cost advantage. Score is 7 due to: (a) strong validated commercial vendor ecosystem with 8+ active vendors selling event planner databases with 90-day update cycles and multi-region coverage (US, UK, Canada, Australia, EMEA, APAC) indicating robust international demand, (b) strong buyer LTV across four primary segments (event software $6K-$350K LTV, venue commissions $500-$20K per event justifying $500-$2K marketing, vendor services $50K-$500K/year recurring from planner relationships, event technology $50K-$500K/year for corporate planners) where one customer acquisition justifies 5×-1,000× database cost, (c) large TAM (80K-120K professional event planning companies generating 150K-250K decision-maker contacts across wedding, corporate, non-profit, and party planning segments), (d) strong industry fundamentals (weddings recovering post-pandemic with 2.5M weddings/year in US at average $30,000 spend = $75B wedding industry, corporate events and conferences resuming in-person with hybrid virtual components driving technology adoption, experiential marketing growing as brands invest in live activations), and (e) absence of low-cost flat-file alternatives creating clear wedge pricing opportunity at $79-$99. Score not higher than 7 due to: (a) fragmented public data sources (no occupational licensing for event planners in most states, requiring aggregation across business registries, directories, certification holders, and venue vendor lists rather than centralized regulatory database), (b) moderate engineering complexity to compile national dataset from multiple sources and classify specializations accurately, (c) high industry fragmentation with mix of established full-time event planning companies (target high-value segment) and part-time/hobbyist coordinators doing 1-5 events/year (lower value long-tail), and (d) challenges in data freshness and accuracy as many event planners operate as sole proprietorships or side businesses without permanent business listings (higher churn than licensed professional industries), though established planners doing 20+ events/year represent stable high-value target.

data_wanted: Secretary of State business entity registrations: Search LLC and corporation databases across all 50 states filtering for event planning business name patterns ("[name] Events", "[name] Event Planning", "[name] Weddings", "[name] Wedding Planning", "[name] Party Planning", "[name] Conference Management", "[name] Event Design", "[name] Celebrations") — business filings contain legal name, DBA, business address, registered agent, entity type, filing date, status (active/dissolved). City and county business license registries: Scrape business license databases (available online in major cities) for event planning, wedding coordinator, and party planning service categories. Industry certification holder directories: Certified Meeting Professional (CMP) credential holders published by Events Industry Council at eventscouncil.org, Certified Special Events Professional (CSEP) designees from International Special Events Society ISES at ises.com, Certified Wedding Planner (CWP) from Wedding Planning Institute, other event industry certifications. Business directory aggregation: Google Business listings for "event planners", "wedding planners", "corporate event planners", "party planners" by city (scrape business name, category, address, phone, website, hours, review count indicating active operation and client volume), Yelp event planning and wedding planning categories with business profiles and contact info, The Knot vendor directory (theknot.com/marketplace) and WeddingWire directory (weddingwire.com/vendors) containing 100,000+ wedding industry vendors including wedding planners with detailed public profiles showing service areas, pricing, portfolio photos, and contact information, Zola wedding vendors, Eventective venue and vendor search. Venue preferred vendor lists: Many hotels, conference centers, and wedding venues publish recommended or exclusive event planner lists on their websites — scrape venue sites and preferred vendor pages. Industry association member directories: Meeting Professionals International (MPI) at mpi.org member search, International Live Events Association (ILEA) at ileahub.com member directory, National Association of Catering and Events (NACE) at nace.net member listings, American Society of Association Executives (ASAE) at asaecenter.org for association event planners, Wedding International Professionals Association (WIPA) members, Association of Bridal Consultants (ABC) members. Website scraping and social media: Instagram wedding planner accounts (typically use #weddingplanner, #eventplanner hashtags and have business contact in bio), LinkedIn profiles for "Event Planner", "Wedding Coordinator", "Conference Manager" with company affiliations, Pinterest wedding planning boards linked to planner businesses, Facebook business pages for event planning companies. Target fields per event planning business: Company/business name and DBA, owner or lead planner name(s), business mailing address, office location (if different from mailing), phone number, email address (scraped from website contact pages or business directory listings), website URL, specialization and event types served (wedding planner, corporate event planner, non-profit fundraiser coordinator, social event planner, party planner, conference and meeting planner, trade show coordinator, festival organizer, experiential marketing, concert and entertainment events), service area or geographic coverage (local city, regional, national, destination events), industry certifications (CMP, CSEP, CWP, others), professional association memberships (MPI, ILEA, NACE, ASAE, WIPA, ABC), approximate annual event volume (where stated on website "planning 50+ weddings annually" or estimated from portfolio size, testimonials count, team size), company size or team member count, years in business or established date, vendor partnerships and preferred vendor status at specific venues, social media handles (Instagram, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Facebook), and client review ratings (from Google, The Knot, WeddingWire indicating reputation and volume). Classify event planners by primary specialization: wedding and social events (most common, 30,000-40,000 planners), corporate events and conferences (20,000-30,000 including association event managers, corporate meeting planners, incentive trip coordinators), non-profit and fundraising events (10,000-15,000 managing charity galas, auctions, golf tournaments, walkathons), party and milestone celebrations (10,000-15,000 focusing on birthday parties, anniversaries, bar/bat mitzvahs, quinceañeras, retirement parties), and specialized events (10,000-20,000 managing festivals, concerts, sporting events, trade shows, experiential brand activations, product launches). Further segment by company size/volume: micro planners (1-10 events/year, often part-time or starting out), small planners (11-30 events/year, full-time independent or small team), medium planners (31-75 events/year, established company with 3-10 person team), and large/enterprise planners (75+ events/year, national firms or destination management companies with 10+ employees). Target all active event planning businesses with emphasis on established planners doing 20+ events/year (higher-value segment for software vendors, venues, and suppliers). Approximately 100,000-150,000 total event planning businesses and independent coordinators in US: includes 80,000-120,000 professional event planning companies (primary target) plus 20,000-30,000 venue-employed event coordinators (hotel catering/event managers, conference center coordinators). Target output: 120,000-180,000 rows (includes individual planners at multi-planner firms appearing as separate contacts, plus venue coordinators who also make vendor purchasing decisions). Data is partially public: business entity registrations and business licenses are public records, industry certification holders publish member directories, business directory listings (Google, Yelp) are publicly scrapable, The Knot and WeddingWire vendor profiles are open-access public directories, venue preferred vendor lists are published on venue websites, and association member directories are often searchable online — however no centralized occupational licensing database exists for event planners (most states do not license this profession), requiring aggregation across multiple public and semi-public sources to achieve comprehensive national coverage with classification by specialization.
